content.title: The emotional landscape of retirement: Planning for life, not just money
content.text: Financial readiness alone doesn’t guarantee satisfaction or a life well-lived in retirement. Many retirees and those soon-to-be experience emotional transitions – a shift from structured work life to self-directed time that can bring both exhilaration and uncertainty.Retirement is both a finish line and the beginning of a new life chapter. The financial aspects of retirement are pretty straight forward. Primary questions include what’s your number (what you need to retire and stay retired), what “surprises” did you overlook, how to convert your nest egg to a cash flow that’ll last a lifetime, and when and how to elect retirement benefits. But the questions shouldn't stop there.Brian Loy Beyond the numbers, retirement invites a different kind of preparation: embracing the transition from diligent saver to confident spender, rediscovering passions, and intentionally shaping days filled with purpose, connection, and joy. At its best, this stage of life is not about slowing down, but about living with clarity, resilience, and a renewed sense of well-being.What are you retiring to?In his book “New Retirementality,” Mitch Anthony discusses the importance of practice and mental preparation, and that the advertised life of leisure isn’t what it’s cracked up to be. He writes about the dangers of golfing every day (my apologies to avid golfers): “First you get bored. Then worse, you become boring.” The moral is not about golf, but rather "don’t become boring." What’s your next great purpose in life? Where to re-channel your energy and passion? Think of your value and continued ability to make a difference. How many 25-year-olds does it take to replace 30 or 40 years of expertise, experience, and connections? What if you re-tooled (new vocation) or re-trained (new knowledge and insights)? A new career, running for office, volunteering, or mentoring to name a few. Look at seniors who continue to work – some have financial needs; however, others do it for social engagement or sense of purpose.Shifting from Saver to Spender For those hard-wired to save, it can be hard to shift, and to spend hard earned savings. That’s understandable. However, it can manifest into two related challenges in retirement: I’m only spending earnings on my savings, and I do not want to tap principal. Income only investing may work short term but may be strained longer term from periods of low interest rates – it was not that long ago that yields on savings accounts were close to zero – and rising costs of living – inflation. Inflation has been called “a hidden menace” in retirement because it erodes purchasing power. Say you can earn $40,000 a year from interest and dividends on $1 million savings. However, if inflation averages 3% annually, that $40,000 is only worth half as much in about 24 years (think the Rule of 72 which tells you how long it takes money to double at a specific return... in this case, divide 72 by 3 and you get 24). Hence, prudent investors think “total return” from their investments – income yield plus capital appreciation – and it is ok to spend principal when your savings need to stretch three or four decades in retirement. And besides the financial aspect of sustainability, there is the emotional question of how much is enough. Think of two bumper stickers – “She who dies with the most toys wins” and “We SKI – Spending our kids' inheritance.” It’s often a balance of having enough wealth for “just in case” (we live longer than expected, need for healthcare or assisted living, etc.) and “you can’t take it with you.”Healthy HabitsA wise person told me to choose activities in retirement that provide one of 5 things:It makes you money.It makes you move and exercise.It keeps you engaged. It challenges your mind.Or it brings you joy.There are some retirees with full calendars – travel, family, sport, volunteering and hobbies – and amazed they once held full-time careers. These are the reasons one saves, sacrifices and maintains discipline. The question of what’s important about money to you may very well be security, having options and flexibility to do the things you want to do, and possibly to be a good steward until it’s time to pass it on to your heirs and causes or charities that are important to you.Life can get complicated with finances and emotions. That is why it pays to have a financial plan, a roadmap, and trusted advisors to help you navigate life and the surprises she gives us. Know where you’re at and where you’re going. Periodically check your progress and adjust along the way. May you have sage advice and secure your future wisely.Brian Loy, CFA, CFP is a financial adviser and Managing Director in the Reno office of Wealthspire Advisors.
